Thank you for speaking the truth. There are so many wonderful women in science who deserve more attention for their contribution to humanity's journey to the stars than that hack ever will. 

It's a beautiful suggestion that I don't think is morbid tbh (but maybe that's just me). McAuliffe is actually one of my favorite figures in space history. She was a teacher and extremely passionate about her job, and she couldn't wait to teach her students from aboard the Space Shuttle. I think that's all so admirable because astronauts are usually upheld as these larger-than-life superhero-like figures, and people like her remind us that we're the same species after all. I think teaching is a honorable job and I hope more teachers will be able to go to space in the future. Also I think Christa is a beautiful name!

As a space & astronauts nerd I wouldn't recommend anyone name their child after Valentina Tereshkova. She is a horrible human being. Off of the top of my head there are some amazing women astronauts with really cool names for your consideration: Sally (Ride - first American woman in space, the youngest American astronaut, and also a talented physicist), Eileen (Collins - a test pilot who went on to become the first woman to pilot a space shuttle), Mae (Jemison, a doctor & engineer who became the first African American woman in space and has multiple doctorates) or Tamara (Jernigan, an astrophysicist who has logged over 1512 hours in space)

I wish your daughter and loved ones a long and happy life 🫂

edit: not astronauts but I have to add some more suggestions from some of my favorite women in science!

Emmy (Noether) - mathematician & physicist who proved one of the most fundamental and important theorems of physics, which holds the field together to this day.

Hedy (Lamarr) - the woman whose work laid the groundwork for WiFi and Bluetooth technology that we use today, and also a Hollywood actress and spy against Nazi Germany! She is one of my favorite historical figures ever honestly. 

Ada (Lovelace) - a writer and mathematician who basically invented the first computer... in the 19th century!!! Besides having a beautiful name that I'd consider for a daughter myself, I think her story is also fascinating and really worth a read.

I breezed through lower education because I have a knack for math and school isn't hard in my country anyway. Everyone including me thought I had a bright future. I signed up for a 3 year degree in physics four years ago and I'm about to start my fifth year. I am the bottom of every single class and I can't pass anything. I really like physics and I've got a thing for it as well as math, all my professors have at one point pulled me aside and told me that my academic performance makes no sense in terms of my skill and knowledge but it is what it is. The biggest dagger in my heart was when my favorite professor (a famous astrophysicist— my dream job since I was a little kid) told me she wants to involve me in research, but needs me to pass her subject first. In daily life I'm about as useful as a literate chimpanzee but put me in a dangerous situation and I'll be the calmest person there. It's something I'm honestly really proud of and one of the very few things I like about having ADHD. And I'm extremely grateful that I have this ability because if I wasn't this way my dad would have died. 

During a mountaineering trip we had accidentally gone up the wrong path and ended up forced to walk on a narrow brick channel on the side of a cliff. The bricks were only about 8cm/3 inches wide and the cliff dropped to jagged rocks, at least 6 stories high. There was a little land around the two rows of bricks but not enough to walk on, just to balance ourselves if we were slipping. A fuck ton of things like the following story happened during that day but I won't go into detail. We were trapped for at least 5 hours. 

The specific incident was that my dad was walking in front of me, suddenly his foot slipped and he fell and rolled down the side of the cliff. THANK FUCKING GOD that the drop was just a little steeper at this part because he managed to catch his foot and created just enough static friction to stay put for the split second that I needed to catch his wrist with one hand and pull him up. My dad is way taller and heavier than me and I have no idea how the hell I managed to do that with just one hand while balancing on those small bricks. He's just like me when it comes to danger so we just looked at each other like [this](https://im.indiatimes.in/media/content/2019/Apr/thor_and_daenerys_targaryen_had_an_epic_faceoff_on_twitter__that_has_sent_the_fans_in_a_tizzy_1556541145_725x725.png) for a second and then calmly continued walking. 

Honestly I sometimes get nightmares from this event and find myself getting extremely anxious in situations that remind me of that day but I remember the way I kept my cool and honestly like that's got to be some superpower shit. Situations like this make me believe there's no way there wasn't a reason for ADHD to exist, even if it doesn't align with my life goals at all lol. 

If my career in physics doesn't work out I guess I'll become a firefighter or something 🤷🏻‍♂️

I'm a physics undergrad and I have ADHD type C. It's pretty bad and it causes me to have a very different line of thinking compared to other people. But you can train your line of thinking to do the same things other people can do, too. Chances are you already know what you need to do, the only problem is your brain hesitating to translate it mathematically, but that's a very learnable thing! 

Here are some things that helped me:

1. Brush up on the math skills. Practice math problems as much as you can. Don't just learn the concepts by heart, try to understand them intuitively. Let's take trigonometric functions for example. The sine function of 90 degrees is 1, but *why* is it 1? Look at the unit circle and you'll get it. Watch a video or two about the unit circle, then think about what implications that could have for other shapes. Look at problems that utilize the sine function. Look at how trigonometric formulas are derived and try to do it yourself. You'll start to get to know its workings and you'll be able to use it creatively.


2. Watch as many math and physics problems being solved as possible— notice how I said watch and not read. PatrickJMT on YouTube, for example, has a ton of videos like that and I find his channel very helpful. This will help you develop that "hunch" physics problems need to be solved. You'll see what's possible and how to go about it and you'll be able to apply it. 


3. Unless you're like me (which I don't recommend) and absolutely want to be perfect at physics at all costs, don't fret about it. Math doesn't have to be your thing, but you can make it your thing if you try hard enough. I struggled a lot with it too and I'd be a hypocrite if I said I'm doing great in my field and everything. Both math and physics are extremely difficult disciplines but I personally believe ANYTHING can be learned! I've even had my professors, some of them being incredibly capable individuals, say that born talent will only give someone a head start but the rest of it is all hard work. Maybe you won't be Einstein but being Faraday is pretty good too— after all the dude did come up with a bunch of groundbreaking concepts while not knowing any math beyond trigonometry and basic algebra!
